content:
Swiss Glaciers Face Unprecedented Melting in 2025

Switzerland's glaciers have experienced a significant 3% reduction in ice volume this year, marking the fourth-largest annual loss on record. This alarming trend is attributed to a combination of low winter snowfall and intense heatwaves during the summer months, particularly in June and August, which were among the warmest on record.

The Rhone Glacier, once Europe's largest, shrank by an average of 1.5 meters in thickness this year alone. Glaciers below 3,000 meters in altitude suffered the most, including the Silvretta Glacier, which endured record-low snowfall in 100 years. The rapid melting not only affects the glaciers themselves but also destabilizes surrounding mountains, increasing the risk of dangerous avalanches and landslides.

Scientists warn that even if global climate stabilizes now, most glaciers will continue to shrink. However, up to 200 high-altitude Swiss glaciers could still be saved if global carbon emissions are reduced to net zero over the next 30 years. The ongoing glacier retreat has significant implications for hydropower, tourism, agriculture, and water supply across Europe.
